clue.text: Exuberance of black cat

parts.note: B is the standard abbreviation for black, as on pencils
the ounce is another name for the snow leopard, a big cat

explanation.surface: Someone admires the lively spirit of a black cat.
explanation.definitionFit: Bounce is liveliness or vigour, a close synonym of exuberant energy.

clue.text: Recurrent Gibraltar issue escalating greatly

indicators.note: recurrent is read as running back, so the abbreviation for Gibraltar is written backwards
escalating means going up, and in a down clue a word going up is read from the bottom

parts.note: to issue is to emit or send out

explanation.surface: A long-running political dispute over Gibraltar keeps intensifying.
explanation.walkthrough: Both 'Recurrent' and 'escalating' are reversal signals; 'escalating' works because this is a down clue, where going up means reading backwards.
explanation.definitionFit: The informal phrase is an adverb meaning hugely or to a great degree, as in 'messed up in a big way'.

clue.text: Aunt Georgia oddly lacking internal organs

indicators.note: the odd-numbered letters of these two words are dropped, so only the even ones are kept

explanation.surface: Aunt Georgia, it seems, is missing some of her internal organs.
explanation.definitionFit: The plural of the Latin name for the womb, an organ inside the body.

clue.text: Fancy a hundred and thirty days on frozen water?

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
April has thirty days; APR is its abbreviation
ice is frozen water

explanation.surface: A whimsical idea: spending a hundred and thirty days out on the ice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on' in a down clue means the pieces stack above ICE. 'Thirty days hath September, April, June and November' is the rhyme behind the April abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A caprice is a sudden whim, and fancy as a noun is a passing notion or whim.

clue.text: Starts to open wine after top award

indicators.note: after places the picked letters behind the word for top

parts.note: top as an adjective means best, the highest in quality

indicators.note: starts to means the opening letter of each of the following words is taken

explanation.surface: Instructions to uncork the wine once the top prize has been handed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top award' reads as one phrase but splits: 'top' is BEST and 'award' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To award something is to confer or present it, the same as to bestow.

clue.text: Gentleman enquiring about house paint

indicators.note: about signals turning round, so the concealed letters are read backwards
house means contain, so the clue words hold the letters inside them

explanation.surface: A gentleman is asking about paint for his house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' looks like what is being painted but is the verb 'contain': LEMANE sits inside 'Gentleman enquiring', and 'about' reverses it.
explanation.definitionFit: Enamel is a glossy hard-drying type of paint, so it is a kind of the defining word.

clue.text: Custom of not returning to collect bones over time

indicators.note: to collect means to gather in, so the reversed word holds the rest inside it
returning means coming back, so the word not is read backwards
over is read as covering, so the bones go round the letter for time

parts.note: the radii are forearm bones, plural of radius

explanation.surface: A habit of never going back to pick up old bones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'returning' makes TON from 'not'; 'over' wraps RADII round T to give RADITI; 'to collect' puts that inside TON.
explanation.definitionFit: A custom is an established practice handed down, which is what a tradition is.

clue.text: Massive wife, four fifths of a ton

parts.note: a ton is slang for a hundred, and four fifths of a hundred is eighty

explanation.surface: An unkind remark about a very heavy wife, nearly a ton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ton' looks like a weight but is the slang for a hundred, so four fifths of it is EIGHTY.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe something of great weight or heft.

clue.text: Frank tore after dog in DC

indicators.note: after puts the word for tore behind the word for dog

parts.note: frank means plain-spoken or direct
a cur is a mongrel dog
rent is an old past tense of rend, to tear

explanation.surface: A man named Frank chasing a dog around Washington DC.
explanation.walkthrough: DC looks like Washington, District of Columbia, but is the electrical abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: DC is the standard abbreviation for the one-way electrical flow, as opposed to AC.

clue.text: I retired, nursing left eye

indicators.note: nursing means holding close, so one piece is placed inside the other
retired means drawn back, so the word for I is read backwards

parts.note: ego is Latin for I, the self

explanation.surface: A retiree tending a sore left eye.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' turns EGO into OGE, which then holds L.
explanation.definitionFit: Eye used as a verb means to look at, and to ogle is to look at lustfully.

clue.text: Arachne engulfed by a campfire, accidentally as it first seems

indicators.note: engulfed by means swallowed up within, so the setter's letter goes inside the rearranged letters
accidentally suggests letters fallen out of order, so they are rearranged

parts.note: Arachne is the setter's pseudonym, so the setter is I

explanation.surface: The setter, Arachne, caught up in a campfire by accident.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themself usually stands for I or ME; here it is I placed among the anagram of A CAMPFIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means on first appearance, before closer examination.

clue.text: British family on island initially imprisoned for skimpy clothing

indicators.note: on in an across clue means placed after, so the word for family follows the island letter

parts.note: kin means family or relatives

indicators.note: initially means the first letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: A British family on an island are locked up for wearing too little.
explanation.definitionFit: A bikini is a two-piece swimsuit, very brief clothing.

clue.text: Seeing quite boring people rowing

indicators.note: boring means drilling into, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: an eight is a racing crew of eight rowers
quite is used as a reply of agreement, meaning yes

explanation.surface: Some find watching rowers rather tedious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quite boring' looks like 'rather dull' but 'boring' means piercing: YES goes into EIGHT.
explanation.definitionFit: Seeing as a noun is the faculty of vision.

clue.text: Magic words to stir Tory sheep

indicators.note: to stir means to mix up, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Phrases meant to rouse Conservative followers who vote like sheep.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the conjuror's exclamation said as a trick is revealed.

clue.text: Thick-skinned beast, Mr Hyde on rampage after cover-up

indicators.note: after puts the rearranged letters behind the reversed word
up in a down clue means read from bottom to top, so the word is reversed

parts.note: a cap is a covering or lid

indicators.note: on rampage means running wild, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mr Hyde, the monstrous alter ego, runs amok after a scandal is hushed up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover-up' reads as concealment but splits in two, with 'up' acting as a reversal signal in this down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a dated zoological term for large thick-skinned mammals such as elephants.

clue.text: Fool around with unknown Lilliputian

indicators.note: around means turned round, so the word for fool is reversed

parts.note: a nit is a fool, short for nitwit
in algebra unknowns are x, y and z; Y is one

explanation.surface: Someone messing about with a stranger from Lilliput.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of Lilliput in Gulliver's Travels are minute, so the adjective means very small.

clue.text: Voicing full agreement

indicators.note: voicing means saying out loud, so the word is taken by its sound

parts.note: packed means full, crammed

explanation.surface: Speaking in total agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'full agreement' looks like one phrase, but 'full' gives PACKED and 'agreement' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A pact is a formal agreement or treaty.

clue.text: Foul pole vault leaving Virginia seething

indicators.note: seething means churning, so the remaining letters are stirred into a new order
leaving means departing, so those letters are taken out

parts.note: VA is the postal abbreviation for the US state of Virginia

explanation.surface: An athlete fumes after a pole vault deemed foul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foul' looks like a sporting adjective but is the verb. Removing VA from POLE VAULT leaves POLEULT, which 'seething' rearranges.
explanation.definitionFit: To foul something is to make it dirty, which is what to contaminate or poison means.

clue.text: Alcoholic drink is truly an evil

indicators.note: evil is read as corrupted or bad, so these letters are twisted into another order

explanation.surface: A moralist declares that drink really is a wickedness.
explanation.definitionFit: A cocktail of Scotch whisky and Drambuie goes by this name.

clue.text: Drinker finally ejected from hot and humid local

indicators.note: ejected from means thrown out of, so a letter is removed

parts.note: tropical describes hot and humid weather

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A drinker thrown out of a stuffy pub.
explanation.walkthrough: 'local' looks like the British word for a regular pub but is the adjective. 'finally' gives R, which leaves TROPICAL.
explanation.definitionFit: In medicine a treatment applied to one area is described as local, applied to the surface.

clue.text: Kiddies regularly team up, in theory

indicators.note: regularly means every other letter of the word is taken

parts.note: to ally is to join forces or team up

explanation.surface: Children routinely pair off, in principle at least.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true in an ideal world but perhaps not in practice holds in theory.

clue.text: Grandma's tent out of bounds for Arctic explorer

parts.note: nan is an informal word for grandmother, with the possessive s

indicators.note: out of bounds means the boundaries are dropped, so only the middle of the word is kept

explanation.surface: Grandma's tent is off limits to the polar adventurer.
explanation.definitionFit: Fridtjof Nansen was a Norwegian who explored the Arctic and crossed Greenland.

clue.text: Act honourably and skin fruit for Spooner

indicators.note: Spooner is known for swapping the opening sounds of words, so these two words exchange initial sounds

parts.note: to flay is to strip the skin off
a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A call to behave decently, followed by a gruesome cookery instruction.
explanation.walkthrough: FLAY PEAR with the F and P swapped is spoken as the answer; the swap goes by sound because PEAR and PAIR rhyme with FAIR.
explanation.definitionFit: To act honourably is to behave fairly and keep to the rules.

clue.text: Puts spikes behind back of Co-op

indicators.note: behind puts the drink word after the picked letter
back of means the final letter of the word is taken

parts.note: to spike a drink is to lace it with alcohol

explanation.surface: Someone sets out sharp objects behind the back of the Co-op shop.
explanation.walkthrough: The Co-op is a chain of British shops.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something somewhere is to place it, so both verbs mean set down.

clue.text: Places book of vacuous theatrical anecdotes under "A"

indicators.note: under in a down clue puts the picked letters below the capital letter
vacuous means empty, so the insides of the words are discarded, leaving their outer letters

explanation.surface: A book of hollow luvvie anecdotes is filed under the letter A.
explanation.definitionFit: A book of maps shows places of the world.

clue.text: Playing percussion very fast

indicators.note: playing suggests the letters being played about with, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A drummer playing at frantic speed.
explanation.definitionFit: Supersonic means faster than the speed of sound, an extreme of speed.

clue.text: Lie about money being short

indicators.note: being short means cut off at the end, so the last letter goes

parts.note: lolly is British slang for money

explanation.surface: Fibbing about cash when one is hard up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lie about' looks like 'tell untruths' but means lounge.
explanation.definitionFit: To loll is to sprawl lazily, lounging or lying around.

clue.text: Fur coat stolen from Merc store

indicators.note: coat stolen from means the outer layer of the word is removed, keeping its middle

parts.note: a mine is a store, a rich source of supply

explanation.surface: A fur coat taken from a Mercedes car showroom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fur coat' reads as one item, but 'coat stolen from Merc' strips M and C to leave ER. Merc is a short name for a Mercedes car.
explanation.definitionFit: Ermine is the white winter fur of the stoat, used on robes.

clue.text: Sentimental drunk wearing Y-fronts inside out and back to front

indicators.note: wearing means having on, so the outer pair surrounds the drunk
back to front means reversed, so the pair of letters is read the other way
inside out is read as the insides taken out, leaving only the outer letters

parts.note: a lush is a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A tipsy man soppily wearing his underpants inside out and back to front.
explanation.walkthrough: Y-fronts are British men's briefs. 'inside out' leaves Y and S; 'back to front' makes SY, which goes round LUSH.
explanation.definitionFit: Slushy is an informal word for mawkishly sentimental, like gushing romantic writing.
